issues.legal_issue: A criminal court must consider victim compensation in every criminal case and disclose its consideration through reasons, even though the ultimate award or refusal remains discretionary.
material_facts: The trial court imposed sentences, which the appellate court later set aside in part and replaced with probation and a fine payable to the victim.
The Sessions Court and High Court did not adequately address the need to compensate the injured complainant.
issues.conclusion: The court held that criminal courts have a duty to apply their minds to compensation in every criminal case and to give reasons showing that they have done so.
issues.legal_principle: Section 357 CrPC confers a power coupled with a duty to consider compensation in every criminal case; the court must record reasons demonstrating its consideration. Section 357-A provides for State-funded compensation where compensation under Section 357 is inadequate or the victim needs rehabilitation. The court relied on Ankush Shivaji Gaikwad v. State of Maharashtra, including its discussion of Hari Singh v. Sukhbir Singh; State of A.P. v. Polamala Raju; Maya Devi v. Raj Kumari Batra; Julius v. Lord Bishop of Oxford; and Suresh v. State of Haryana.

predicates.criminal_sentencing_proceeding: A court is deciding sentence or compensation in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.victim_suffered_loss_or_injury: The offence caused a victim loss or injury.

issues.definition: When a court is sentencing in a criminal proceeding involving a victim who suffered loss or injury, it must consider compensation and record reasons for its decision.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court may order victim compensation despite the absence of detailed evidence quantifying the victim’s losses, and may do so instead of imposing ordinary imprisonment or retaining a fine where the circumstances warrant that remedy.
material_facts: The complainant had sustained multiple injuries, including wounds described as muscle-deep and bone-deep.
There was no evidence establishing the complainant’s medical expenses or loss of earnings, and there was no evidence of the accused’s financial capacity.
A substantial period had passed since the offence, and the court considered ordinary imprisonment inappropriate at that stage.
The lower courts had imposed a fine payable to the victim but had not adequately addressed compensation.
issues.conclusion: The court ordered the surviving accused to pay compensation to the complainant, with imprisonment in default of payment, and set aside the fine. It considered ordinary imprisonment inappropriate in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 357 CrPC, just compensation is assessed with regard to matters such as medical and other expenses, pain and suffering, loss of earnings, and the accused’s financial capacity. Where evidence on relevant matters is unavailable, some estimation may be necessary; the court must have adequate material and consider the accused’s capacity, with a summary inquiry where required. Section 357-A provides for State-funded compensation to make up a shortfall where compensation under Section 357 is insufficient. The court relied on Ankush Shivaji Gaikwad v. State of Maharashtra, including its discussion of Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab, Balraj v. State of U.P., Baldev Singh v. State of Punjab, and Dilip S. Dahanukar v. Kotak Mahindra Co. Ltd.; and on K.A. Abbas H.S.A. v. Sabu Joseph.

predicates.victim_appeal_challenges_sentence_or_com: A victim brings an appeal challenging the sentence or the treatment of compensation in a criminal case.
predicates.victim_sustained_injuries: The victim sustained injuries as a result of the offence.
predicates.long_delay_since_offence: A substantial period elapsed between the offence and the reviewing court’s decision.
predicates.no_detailed_evidence_of_loss_or_payment_: The record lacks detailed evidence of the victim’s financial losses or the offender’s capacity to pay.

issues.definition: When a victim appeals the sentencing or compensation outcome, has sustained injuries, the case comes before the court after a substantial delay, and detailed evidence of losses or payment capacity is lacking, the court may order compensation instead of ordinary imprisonment and a fine.
